history.summary: The Kailasanathar Temple is the oldest structural temple in Kanchipuram and the first structural temple built in South India, commissioned by Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) between 685 and 705 CE, with the front facade and gopuram completed by his son Mahendravarman III; earlier Pallava temples were rock-cut (e.g. Mahabalipuram). Built of sandstone on a granite foundation on the banks of the Vedavathi River, it became the model for later Dravidian temples and is said to have inspired Raja Raja Chola I before he built the Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur. The compound holds 58 small shrines of Shiva in niches on the inner face of the circumambulatory wall, many half-animal deities typical of early Dravidian art, early Pallava Sanskrit and Tamil inscriptions, and a famous low crawl passageway around the sanctum symbolizing the cycle of life, death and rebirth. Local tradition holds a secret escape tunnel for wartime kings. The temple is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).

town_description: Kanchipuram, about 72 km southwest of Chennai, is one of Hinduism's seven holiest cities (Sapta Puri) and the 'City of a Thousand Temples', famed for Shiva and Vishnu temples and its silk sarees.

travel.airport: Chennai International Airport, about 75 km away.
travel.railway: Kanchipuram Railway Station, about 3 km from the temple.
travel.road: Well-connected by NH48 from Chennai and Bengaluru; TNSTC and private buses run regularly.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March; mornings or evenings (stone floors get very hot in the afternoon).
